note.specFocus: Different structures and forms of ordained and lay leadership across Christian denominations.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
1.3 Leadership in the Church
Christian denominations organise leadership differently, reflecting different beliefs about authority and tradition.
Ordained ministry
• Ordination, often through the "laying on of hands", formally sets a person apart to lead worship, preach, teach and administer sacraments such as the Eucharist.
• Catholic and Orthodox churches maintain a hierarchy of deacons, priests and bishops, with the Pope leading the worldwide Catholic Church; this reflects belief in apostolic succession — unbroken leadership passed down from Jesus' original apostles.
• Many Protestant churches have simpler structures, with ministers elected or appointed by the local congregation, reflecting the Reformation-era idea of the "priesthood of all believers" — that every Christian has direct access to God.
Debates in leadership
• Ordination of women: many Anglican and Protestant denominations now ordain women as priests or ministers; the Catholic and Orthodox churches ordain only men, citing tradition and their interpretation of scripture.
• Lay leadership: many churches rely heavily on lay (non-ordained) people for prayer groups, Sunday school and pastoral care, showing leadership is not only exercised by the ordained.
Exam link: "Discuss" questions about leadership reward comparing ordained authority (sacraments, apostolic succession) against lay/congregational involvement (priesthood of all believers), not simply describing one church's structure.

questions.examTip: Make two separate points and develop each one. Link the development directly to the question.
questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Ordained ministers, such as priests or ministers, are formally set apart through ordination, often involving the laying on of hands, to lead worship, preach, teach and administer sacraments such as the Eucharist.

2. In the Catholic and Orthodox traditions, ordained ministry follows a hierarchy including deacons, priests and bishops, with the Pope as leader of the worldwide Catholic Church, while many Protestant churches have simpler structures with ministers elected or appointed by the local congregation.
questions.question: Outline two features of ordained ministry in the Christian Church.

questions.examTip: For 6 marks, combine accurate knowledge with explanation. Explain why each point matters and link it directly to the question; avoid simply listing facts.
questions.modelAnswer:
A developed answer could explain the issue through three connected points.

First, Catholic and Orthodox churches maintain apostolic succession, the belief that bishops are successors of Jesus' original apostles, giving their leadership structure, with the Pope at its head, a particular claim to continuity and authority going back to the early Church.

Second, Many Protestant churches rejected parts of this hierarchy during the Reformation, emphasising instead the "priesthood of all believers", the idea that every Christian has direct access to God without necessarily needing an ordained priest to mediate, leading to simpler, often more congregation-led leadership.

Finally, Differences also arise over the ordination of women: some denominations, including many Anglican and Protestant churches, now ordain women as priests or ministers, while the Catholic and Orthodox churches continue to ordain only men, reflecting different interpretations of scripture and tradition.
questions.question: Explain why there are different forms of leadership in the Christian Church.

questions.examTip: For a 10-mark discussion, analyse different aspects of the Christian issue and how they interrelate. Finish with a reasoned conclusion; do not just list advantages and disadvantages.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Many Christians argue that ordination sets a person apart through training, vocation and the laying on of hands, giving them particular authority and responsibility to administer sacraments such as the Eucharist and to guide a congregation reliably in doctrine.

A second consideration is: Having recognised, ordained leadership can help maintain consistency and unity across a denomination, ensuring that worship and teaching remain faithful to that church's beliefs rather than varying unpredictably from person to person.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Other Christians, especially in traditions that stress the "priesthood of all believers", argue that since the Holy Spirit can work through any believer, lay people should be able to lead prayer, preach and even lead small worship gatherings, not only ordained clergy.

A further consideration is: In practice, many churches already rely heavily on lay leadership for activities such as leading prayer groups, Sunday school and pastoral visiting, showing that meaningful Christian worship and ministry do not always require ordination.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: the answer often depends on whether the focus is on sacramental acts traditionally reserved for ordained leaders, or on the wider life of prayer, teaching and service where lay involvement is already widespread and valued. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.
questions.question: Discuss whether only ordained leaders should lead Christian worship.

questions.examTip: Use accurate Christian teaching, explain why each point matters, and in an evaluation compare arguments before reaching a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of ordained ministry, bishops, priests, pastors, apostolic succession and service and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
